query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, differential atomic mobility during heating leads to local elemental segregation at the surface that forms a disordered, liquid‐like layer (premelting) at temperatures well below the overall bulk melting point. This staggered melting behavior is governed by the intrinsic differences in elemental diffusion and melting temperatures, which are accentuated by the high configurational entropy.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with a homogenized chemical distribution.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled heating with varied ramp rates and, subsequently, cooling under inert conditions to examine the onset and progression of premelting phenomena.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert atmosphere with a temperature ramp that spans below to above the bulk melting point—focusing on the regime between approximately 70% and 90% of the bulk melting temperature—and with controlled cooling rates to probe kinetic effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of a chemically heterogeneous, disordered surface layer (liquid-like skin) induced by elemental segregation.
generation.mechanism: During heating, elements with lower melting points and/or higher diffusion coefficients migrate preferentially toward the nanoparticle surface. This segregation creates a disordered, liquid‐like surface layer (premelting) while the core remains solid. The chemical complexity and associated diffusion differences delay complete homogenization upon cooling, thus affecting the consolidation of the solid solution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to monometallic or bimetallic nanoparticles, these high-entropy alloy nanoparticles will exhibit an earlier onset of a disordered, premelted surface layer and a broadened melting transition. The extent of premelting (e.g., the thickness or coverage of the liquid-like layer) will be greater in nanoparticles with more pronounced elemental diffusion differences and at slower cooling rates that allow enhanced surface mobility.
generation.baseline: Monometallic or binary nanoparticles under analogous thermal conditions, which typically show more uniform and abrupt melting without significant premelting surface segregation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis should apply for nanoparticles with significant surface-to-volume ratios (typically <100 nm) where atomic mobility is non-negligible and within a premelting temperature window (approximately 70–90% of the bulk melting point). It may be less applicable if grain sizes are much larger or if rapid quenching completely suppresses surface diffusion.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative impact of individual elemental diffusion coefficients and melting point disparities on the extent of premelting is not fully determined. Additional factors such as strain, particle morphology, or minor impurities might also influence the observed thermal response.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in-situ TEM heating experiments on Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles while simultaneously mapping the elemental distribution using EDS or similar techniques. Compare the thermal response across samples with varied cooling rates. The experiment should monitor the development of surface disorder and local compositional variations as the temperature approaches 70–90% of the bulk melting point.
measurements: TEM imaging to capture morphological changes and the appearance of a liquid-like surface layer
EDS elemental maps to detect and quantify surface segregation
In-situ diffraction to monitor phase-transition signatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, during the controlled heating experiments, no detectable surface elemental segregation or liquid-like premelted layer is observed (i.e., if the nanoparticles exhibit a uniform, bulk-like melting behavior analogous to monometallic/bimetallic nanoparticles), then the hypothesis that differential elemental diffusion and induced surface segregation governs premelting behavior would be decisively falsified.

Evaluation of Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu System and Subsequent Derivation of a Non-Equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu Alloy

Abstract: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). The more the better: on the formation of single-phase high entropy alloy nanoparticles as catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction†

Abstract: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are an important new material class with significant application potential in catalysis and electrocatalysis. The entropy-driven formation of HEA materials requires high temperatures and controlled cooling rates. However, catalysts in general also require highly dispersed materials, i.e., nanoparticles. Only then a favorable utilization of the expensive raw materials can be achieved. Several recently reported HEA nanoparticle synthesis strategies, therefore, avoid the high-temperature regime to prevent particle growth. In our work, we investigate a system of five noble metal single-source precursors with superior catalytic activity for the oxygen reduction reaction. Combining in situ X-ray powder diffraction with multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we address the fundamental question of how single-phase HEA nanoparticles can form at low temperatures.
